title: Quick Sort
tagline: Pick a pivot, partition around it, recurse — the in-place sort that's fast in practice.

intuition.analogy: To organise a room of people by height, pick one person (the pivot) and ask everyone shorter to stand on the left, taller on the right. Now the pivot is in its final spot, and you repeat within each side. Each side is a smaller version of the same problem.
paragraphs: Quick sort flips merge sort's strategy. Instead of doing trivial splits and hard merges, it does a hard split (partitioning) and a trivial combine (nothing — the pieces are already in the right regions). After partitioning, the pivot sits at its final sorted position.

Partitioning is the heart of it: scan the range, moving everything smaller than the pivot to the front. When done, swap the pivot into the boundary. Everything left is smaller, everything right is larger.

With balanced pivots you halve the range each time → O(n log n). With unlucky pivots (e.g. already-sorted input + last-element pivot) you peel off one element at a time → O(n²). Randomising or using median-of-three pivots makes the bad case astronomically unlikely.
intuition.keyIdea: Partition places the pivot in its final position and splits the rest into 'smaller' and 'larger' regions to recurse on.

steps.title: Choose a pivot
steps.detail: A common choice is the last element. Randomised or median-of-three pivots avoid worst-case behaviour on sorted/adversarial inputs.

steps.title: Partition (Lomuto scheme)
steps.detail: Keep a boundary i. Scan j across the range; whenever a[j] < pivot, swap it to position i and advance i. Finally swap the pivot into position i.

steps.title: Recurse on both sides
steps.detail: The pivot at i is final. Recurse on [l, i-1] and [i+1, r]. Recurse into the smaller side first to bound stack depth at O(log n).

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
complexity.timeReason: Balanced partitions give log n levels of O(n) work. Consistently lopsided partitions degrade to quadratic.
complexity.spaceReason: In-place partitioning; recursion stack is O(log n) with the smaller-side-first trick.

pitfalls: Always picking the first/last element as pivot makes sorted input hit the O(n²) worst case — randomise.
Quick sort is not stable; equal elements may be reordered.
Deep recursion on lopsided splits can overflow the stack — recurse into the smaller part, loop on the larger.

rows: No element < 1, boundary stays at index 0
Swap pivot into index 0 — 1 is final
dryRun.clickMoment: After one partition the pivot never moves again. The sort is just 'fix one element's final spot, then conquer the leftovers' applied recursively.

problems.title: Sort an Array
problems.statement: Sort an array; practise an in-place quicksort with random pivots.
problems.hint: Randomise the pivot to dodge the sorted-input worst case.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element
problems.statement: Find the kth largest element in an unsorted array.
problems.hint: Quickselect: partition, then recurse only into the side that contains rank k — average O(n).
